• Price: $1,299
• Available Spring 2027

• Works with calling apps including WhatsApp and Zoom

candidates.text:
chappelle is the most talented stand up comedian of all time. there is no particular clear second place. he's created his entire own category of “chappelle-standup” that’s distinct from “standup comedy”

modern chappelle combines supernatural comedic timing, and possibly the most comfortable presence someone will ever inhabit on a stage, with a bunch of topical stuff that he’s phoning in these days

the trappings of his own life are the source of most of his comedy after his return to the limelight in the 2010s. he leverages his proximity to show business but also his ironic detachment from show business to generate a feeling for the fans that they’re part of the cabal. the audience at these events is unfortunately truly insufferable. it’s a religious gathering for a lot of these people, they’re hanging onto Dave’s every word, they’re laughing before he even says anything, they’re doing rhythmic babble like they’re at some kind of secular liturgy

the guy is old and the superstardom has definitely gotten to him a bit. you see this tendency in many people where to get famous they have to be consistently at their peak hilarity, top performance, and as time goes on the mic becomes a soapbox. happens to many good posters too. it starts with jokes that are funny because you have a worldview and enhanced by your opinions and then transitions to mostly lecturing about your worldview

in these comedy club routines he’s clearly just kind of winging it. there’s not much sense of beginning middle and end. there’s no real through line, unlike his netflix specials which tend to have some sort of exquisite story arc that always lands the joke material he leaves hanging throughout the show. at the live shows, he’s mostly riffing with the audience and his guest star about insider dave-chappelle-superfan-throwback stuff and the general culture, which he still maintains a preternatural finger on the pulse of. he does mention the creation of "digital gods" at one point and a sort of omnicausal sense that the world is ending

even he admits “this is not going well”, and he’s getting progressively drunker as the show ends unceremoniously “damn I need to figure out my closer”. chappelle at 20% power is still somehow the absolute goat. the distribution of human talents is so uneven it’s absurd. it's always a pleasure to observe this level of greatness of any form up close. anyways i need to figure out my closer

candidates.text:
Any product that involves putting in money to get more money out in a short period of time is gambling.

There are many variations of this type of product and people will pretend it’s investing or truth seeking. But really it’s just selling entertainment in the form of gambling.

And the only way that type of entertainment works is when the win/lose ratio is razor thin.

Vegas historically has made trillions on a 1% edge.

But when a business comes along that is selling the same entertainment, but takes a 10, 20, 30% edge, and continues to pretend like it isn’t doing that, it’s really no surprise when customers revolt and take any change they can to demonize it.

Thanks for entertaining my vaguepost.

I've met so many smart people who struggled with their relationships, with their spouse, with their parents, with their children, and it's very obvious why it happens: most of them somehow assumed that these were "side quests" (as opposed to the "main quest" of their career and financial achievements), and they invested their time and energy accordingly, and that was simply just not enough.

Some ambitions require personal sacrifices, but too many people seem to get confused throughout the journey, and start forgetting that “winning” is no winning at all if you destroy all your meaningful bonds with others in the process. When you choose the right timelines and scenarios for your life, it's not lonely at the top, quite the opposite.

"Only tech people will use agents, like Muse/Instinct/Grokbot. Mainstream consumers won't adopt it." 

I can't help but feel like it sounds similar to the early days of ridesharing where the discourse was "people love driving," "taxis already exist," and "calling a black car is a niche, elite thing." 

But Uber made it accessible for everyone to be able to call a car (and to do so in a much less painful way).

Fast forward to now, Uber and Lyft got mainstream adoption. And people remain buying cars and loving to drive. 

I wonder if we'll see agents get mainstream adoption in a similar way (and also like this pain relief framing)
